screens.body: Java likes things spelled out. Every statement ends with a semicolon. Blocks of code sit inside curly braces. And you must declare what type of data a variable holds before you use it. It feels strict at first, but that strictness catches your mistakes early — the compiler is a picky friend who saves you from yourself.
screens.heading: Java likes things spelled out
screens.keyPoint: Semicolons, braces, declared types — Java is explicit.

screens.body: A variable is a labeled box that holds one value. In Java you declare it by naming its type first: int score = 0; makes an integer box called score holding 0. The type locks in what kind of data can go inside — you can't stuff text into an int box later.

options: Make an integer box named score holding 0
check.question: int score = 0; means…

code.snippet:
int score = 0;
score = 15; // the box now holds 15

screens.heading: Variables: labeled boxes
screens.keyPoint: Declare the type, name the box, put a value in.

screens.body: Java's main primitive types cover the basics. int holds whole numbers (19, -3). double holds decimals (19.99, 3.14). boolean holds true or false — nothing else. char holds a single character in single quotes ('A', '7'). Picking the right type is half of declaring variables well.

check.question: Which type holds a decimal number?

screens.heading: The main primitive types
screens.keyPoint: int, double, boolean, char — pick the right box.

screens.body: Operators do the math: + - * / and % (remainder). They follow the order of operations you learned in school — multiplication before addition. One Java gotcha: dividing two ints does integer division, dropping the decimal. 5 / 2 is 2, not 2.5. If you want decimals, at least one side must be a double.
screens.heading: Operators do math
screens.keyPoint: Watch out: int / int drops the decimal.

screens.body: Text lives in Strings — note the capital S, because String is special in Java. You join strings with +, which glues them together. String text always uses double quotes; single quotes are only for single chars. Mixing them up is one of the most common beginner errors.

code.snippet:
String name = "Roli";
String hi = "Hi, " + name; // "Hi, Roli"

screens.heading: Strings: text in quotes
screens.keyPoint: Strings use double quotes; + glues them together.

screens.body: Programs talk to users two ways. System.out.println prints a line to the screen — your output. To read what the user types, you use a Scanner: create one, then call nextLine() to grab a line of input. Input in, output out — the computer loop from topic one.

check.question: To read a line the user typed…

screens.heading: Talking to the user: input & output
screens.keyPoint: println prints out; Scanner reads input in.

screens.body: Names matter more than beginners think. Java convention is camelCase: first word lowercase, each next word capitalized — totalPrice, not totalprice or Total_Price. Names should say what the value is. And // starts a comment: a note to humans that Java ignores. Future you will thank present you for comments.

screens.heading: Names matter
screens.keyPoint: camelCase, meaningful names, comments for humans.
